surfaces.part: top stone of cairn with snow tufts

answer.evidence: The cairn is a stack of dark grey stones seen from the front, with a thin spear shaft standing against its right side. The top stone (rows 12-14, width 6) is a rounded lump with white snow at the corners and no ellipse or front-edge line. The snow on the left of the middle tier (rows 16-18, ending at a darker row 19) is a 2-3 row strip and does not read as a horizontal surface. The rest of the body (rows 15-25) is vertical stone faces, and the base at rows 26-30 is a flat snow drift. The overall impression is a front elevation with at most a rim-like top.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a small cairn of individually shaded stones with a snow cap and a spear. It is much smaller than the tree references, so I judged it by eye as a sparse object as well as by the numbers. It has 24 visible tones per full tile, level with tree-d43edd (29) and well above tree-1a786c (7). Near-flat coverage is 0%, the same as both references, and there are no 5x5 flat fills. Each stone has a light face, mid and dark shading, so I count about 5 steps against roughly 6 on the references. The outline is mixed: 40% of dark edge pixels are near-neutral, so some edges lean black, but the rest are tinted dark stone and shaft tones, so it is not a uniform sticker line. The piece is not thinner or flatter than the references, so a careful artist would likely accept it beside them, though it is not a clear win on outline tint.

surfaces.part: snow cap on top of cairn

answer.evidence: The cairn is a stacked mound of dark grey stones seen face-on, rows 15-25, with a narrow snow cap at rows 12-14 (width 6, then 7-9). The cap is mostly a highlight with no clear edge line or eave shadow, so it reads as a rim and not a real top surface. The stones are lit as vertical faces with no horizontal plane. The width profile widens steadily from 6 to 11 like a mound, not like an ellipse. The spear is a thin vertical shaft, counted as decor. The snow at rows 26-30 is a flat ground drift, not part of the main body.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a tiny cairn of stacked grey stones with a thin spear, roughly 15x20 source pixels, so it is a sparse prop. The measured 24 visible tones per tile and 0% near-flat coverage look good on paper, but they come from a very small, busy area. By eye the stones show only about 3 lightness steps (a pale cap, grey mid, dark base) and are not shaded stone by stone as in the references. The dark edges are 40% near-neutral, so the outline is mixed, with partly black-grey lines giving a mild sticker look, unlike the references, which are 0% neutral and use dark green or brown edges. The spear shaft and tip are thin and flat. Next to the rich, multi-tone leaf clumps of tree-d43edd, a careful artist would find it thinner and flatter, and the stones carry less grain and fewer tones. When in doubt, fail.

surfaces.part: cairn top stone with snow cap

answer.evidence: The cairn (rows 12-25, width 6-10) is stacked dark stones seen face-on. The top is a narrow snow-capped crown of about 2 rows (12-13) with white pixels only at the corners. There is no front-edge line, no eave shadow and no ellipse. The snow patches at rows 17-18 and 26-30 look like vertical highlights or a ground drift, not horizontal surfaces. The spear is a thin vertical pole at x=11 with no top surface. The overall read is a front elevation.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a tiny stacked-stone cairn with a spear, not a tree, bush or canopy, so the tree references are a poor like-for-like comparison. The measured facts are fine: 24 visible tones per tile (references 7 and 29) and 0% near-flat coverage. But 40% of the dark edge pixels are neutral, so the outline is partly near-black rather than consistently a dark tint of the neighbouring material, which leans toward the sticker look. By eye the stones show about 4 lightness steps, with a white highlight cap and dark grey sides, against the reference canopies' 5-6 steps. The small sparse silhouette carries less shaded texture and fewer per-stone and per-leaf clusters than the references. When in doubt, fail.

surfaces.part: spear (shaft and tip) rising above the cairn

answer.evidence: The main body is a stack of dark grey stones from rows 12 to 25, widening from 6 to 10 px, on a white base at rows 26-30 that is 11-16 px wide. The top rows 12-14 are a narrow 6 px cap with a white highlight and no front-edge line, no eave shadow and no ellipse. The stones read as a face-on pile, not a horizontal surface. The spear shaft (x~11, rows 7-25) and its tip (rows 0-3) are a pole rising above the pile, so I count them as decor. The white base is a flat band without a top plane. Overall this is a front elevation with at most a 1-2 row highlight on top.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a tiny stone cairn with a thin spear, not a tree or plant. It is only about 10x15 source pixels, so it has no canopy or trunk ramps to compare with the references' 5-6 step leaf and bark ramps. The measured 24 tones per tile and 0% flat coverage look generous for a piece smaller than one tile, so I judged by eye. The stones read as roughly 3-4 grey and white steps with little per-stone shading or grain. 40% of the dark edge pixels are neutral, and the outline looks like a dark neutral line on the stones and spear shaft, not a tint of the adjacent material, so I rate it mixed. The references are tinted (0% neutral) and carry clustered leaf texture. Set beside them, the cairn looks thinner and more sticker-like. The 24-tone fact does not offset that, because the piece is too small to carry that many visible tones.
